In *People We Meet on Vacation* by Emily Henry, the opening chapter effectively establishes the dual timeline structure with a present-day narrative that reflects on past vacations shared by the main characters, Alex and Poppy. Here's an excerpt from the opening chapter, which gives a glimpse into this alternating structure:

> "Alex drove. Alex always drove. I did the playlists and the snacks and the terrible jokes. Somewhere in a gas-station parking lot in western North Carolina, at three in the morning, I discovered that he had been laughing politely at me for six hours and finally, finally, made him actually laugh. He has a specific laugh that he only lets out when he is genuinely amused, a short, quiet, surprised laugh that begins with a pulled-in breath. It is the single most rewarding sound in the world. I have been chasing it ever since."

This excerpt establishes a nostalgic tone as the narrator reflects on their past experiences with Alex, blending humor with a sense of yearning.

For a representative passage from one of the early flashback sections to highlight the tonal contrast, here's an excerpt from the second chapter where the past vacation memories begin to unfold:

> "That was nine summers ago. This year, for the first time, we were not going to [continue with plans we had made]."

In this section, you can note the shift from the lively present-day banter to a more reflective and bittersweet tone that signifies the weight of their current situation compared to their past adventures.

Both excerpts showcase how Henry navigates between past and present, allowing readers to experience the characters' development and the nostalgia of their friendship. This dual timeline creates a rich narrative texture that could be a focal point in your review.
